text.p: Singapore's combined chemical and petroleum output grew about 10 percent to Singapore $22 billion in 1996, the Economic Development Board (EDB) said on Friday.

But petrochemical production dropped 10.5 percent in value terms, owing to "sluggish product prices" in that year, the EDB said. Overall industry growth was boosted by 14.5 percent growth in the petroleum sector alone. The sector accounted for 55 percent of total output due to soaring product prices.
Petroleum product prices such as diesel, naphtha and jet fuel have risen in recent weeks to trade at new post-Gulf War highs due to strong regional demand for the northern winter.
"However, thinner refining margins due to the increase in supply from new refineries in the region have placed stronger competitive pressures on Singapore refiners," the EDB said in a statement.

Industry sources estimate refiners' basic profit at an average of about U.S.$2.00 for every barrel refined in 1996. Over the year, returns ranged from a loss of around 50 cents in the third quarter to a profit of about $4.00 in the first quarter.
"To further enhance their competitiveness, local refiners are strengthening their manufacturing base by diversifying into lube business and integrating with petrochemicals," the EDB said.

Mobil Oil Singapore will start up a S$372 million lube baseoil plant in the third quarter of 1997. Mobil is also conducting a feasibility study for the construction of a S$1.5 billion ethylene plant which is expected to be ready by 2001.

But over the next two to three years, the petrochemical sector is expected to come under pressure due to a increase in capacity following the start-up of several new plants in the region, including Singapore.

The Petrochemical Corporation of Singapore (PCS), which is due to start up a 515,000 tonne per year ethylene plant in the second quarter of 1997, said 1996 profits would be substantially lower than 1995.
PCS, a 50:50 joint venture between Royal Dutch Shell and a consortium of Japanese companies, currently operates a 450,000 tonne per year ethylene plant.
"1996 profit will be substantially lower than 1995," PCS managing director Takayuki Okada told a news conference on Friday.
He declined to give any indication of how large the reduction in profits would be. In 1995, PCS profits soared to Singapore $92.6 million from $71.1 million in 1994.
Its earnings sank to $16.2 million in 1993 when the industry was in the depths of its most recent cyclical downturn.
Okada told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday that prices would come under pressure in the next two to three years and as a result company profitability will also be affected.
"Prices of key petrochemicals such as polyolefins and paraxylene fell by 10-20 percent globally compared to 1995, resulting in weak margins," the EDB said.
Polyolefins such as polyethylene and polypropylene are downstream products which use the ethylene and propylene produced by PCS.
The EDB said 1997 "growth will remain strong but business conditions especially in petrochemicals, could be impacted by the cyclical nature of the global industry".
